metadata.title: Determinants of Adult Education and Training Participation in the United States: A Machine Learning Approach

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the 2017 U.S. PIAAC microdata and restricts the analytic sample to respondents aged 25–65 with work experience in the last 12 months (N=1,334). The authors state that the U.S. PIAAC data were already stratified by gender, age, education, and income, and therefore they report that weighting was not needed for their analyses. The paper does not report any use of complex survey weights or replicate-weight procedures (e.g., BRR/jackknife), and the ML models (Random Forest classifiers in scikit-learn) are implemented without explicit survey-weight incorporation. As a result, the estimates of variable importance and predictive accuracy should be interpreted as model-based associations within the selected sample rather than fully design-weighted population estimates.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables are binary indicators of job-related formal AET participation and nonformal AET participation (0/1), not cognitive achievement scores with PIAAC plausible values. Therefore, plausible values handling is not applicable to the modeled outcomes. The manuscript does not describe any missing-data handling procedure for predictors or outcomes, which is a reporting gap because ML training typically requires a documented strategy for missingness (e.g., deletion or imputation) to ensure reproducibility.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the 2017 U.S. PIAAC dataset; selected respondents aged 25–65 years who reported work experience in the last 12 months; excluded respondents aged 16–24 to align with the typical adult AET age range. The dependent variables were defined as binary participation in job-related formal AET (past 12 months) and job-related nonformal AET (past 12 months). The paper does not report additional exclusions (e.g., item nonresponse thresholds) or a specific missing-data rule.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIAAC 2017 U.S. (adults 25–65) — job-related formal AET participation
main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest classifier — average testing classification accuracy: 88%.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIAAC 2017 U.S. data (adults 25–65) the study leveraged age and literacy/numeracy/ICT skills use at work (plus work flexibility) to predict formal AET participation (binary), finding that age and literacy skills use at work were the most important factors and that the model achieved an average testing classification accuracy of 88%. This indicates that strengthening adults’ opportunities to apply literacy and related job skills—alongside age-targeted support—may improve uptake of formal, credential-oriented training, though the study reports variable importance rather than causal effects and does not provide a design-weighted estimation strategy.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIAAC 2017 U.S. (adults 25–65) — job-related nonformal AET participation
main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest classifier — average testing classification accuracy: 71%.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIAAC 2017 U.S. data (adults 25–65) the study leveraged literacy/numeracy/ICT skills use at work and organization size (plus monthly income) to predict nonformal AET participation (binary), finding that skills use at work and organization size were the most important factors and that the model achieved an average testing classification accuracy of 71%. This indicates that policies and employer practices that increase day-to-day use of job-relevant skills and provide organizational support (e.g., enabling learning-rich workplaces) may raise participation in nonformal, workplace-based learning, while the results remain predictive associations without causal identification and without documented missing-data handling.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes the 2017 U.S. PIAAC dataset, restricting the sample to adults aged 25–65 who reported work experience in the last 12 months (N=1,334). It models two binary outcomes—job-related formal AET participation and job-related nonformal AET participation—using Random Forest classifiers implemented in scikit-learn, with five-fold cross-validation and permutation-based variable importance. For formal AET, the model achieved an average testing classification accuracy of 88%, with age and literacy skill use at work emerging as the most important factors, followed by numeracy and ICT skill use. For nonformal AET, the model achieved an average testing classification accuracy of 71%, with literacy skill use at work, ICT and numeracy skill use, and organization size as the most important factors. The paper does not report a missing-data handling strategy and does not incorporate complex survey weights in the ML pipeline, so results should be interpreted as predictive associations rather than population-representative causal effects.
